references.text: Isaiah prophesies about God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples: 'for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples' ([ref:Jes 56:7|Isaiah 56:7]). Jesus alludes to this thought when he condemns those who make his Father's house a marketplace.

Zechariah prophesies that on that day there shall no longer be any 'merchant in the house of the Lord, the God of hosts' ([ref:Sak 14:21|Zechariah 14:21]). Jesus fulfills this prophecy by driving out the merchants from the temple.

Jeremiah rebukes the people for having made the Lord's house a 'den of robbers' ([ref:Jer 7:11|Jeremiah 7:11]). The theme of the misuse of the temple as a marketplace is shared with Jesus' action of cleansing the temple.

'For zeal for your house has consumed me' ([ref:Sal 69:10|Psalms 69:10]). This verse is quoted directly in [ref:Joh 2:17|John 2:17] as an explanation of Jesus' action of cleansing the temple, and is thus closely linked to his words about his Father's house.

In Matthew's account of the temple cleansing, Jesus drives out those who buy and sell and says: 'My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers' ([ref:Matt 21:12-13|Matthew 21:12-13]). Parallel account to the temple cleansing in the Gospel of John.

Mark's account of the temple cleansing where Jesus drives out the merchants and says that his house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations ([ref:Mark 11:15-17|Mark 11:15-17]). Synoptic parallel to the temple cleansing in the Gospel of John.

Luke's account of the temple cleansing where Jesus drives out those who sell and says: 'My house shall be a house of prayer' ([ref:Luk 19:45-46|Luke 19:45-46]). Synoptic parallel to the temple cleansing in the Gospel of John.

Jesus calls God his Father, as he does when he refers to the temple as 'my Father's house'. In [ref:Joh 5:17-18|John 5:17-18], the Jews react to Jesus calling God his own Father and thus making himself equal with God.

The Mosaic law prescribes doves as sacrificial animals for those who cannot afford lambs ([ref:3 Mos 12:8|Leviticus 12:8]). Those who sold doves in the temple were selling exactly such sacrificial animals—but Jesus condemns that the trade took place within the temple itself.

The Mosaic law allowed tithes to be exchanged for money for practical purposes when traveling to the sanctuary ([ref:5 Mos 14:25-26|Deuteronomy 14:25-26]). The presence of money changers in the temple can be seen in light of such practice, but Jesus condemns that it has become a commercial enterprise in his Father's house.
